name: Sound Detectives
subtitle: Aural skills and the elements of music
blurb: Ten weeks of listening. You build a toolkit for describing what you hear, use it on jazz, film music and Australian music, and learn to write about music with evidence.

weeks.title: The Elements Toolkit
weeks.intro: Welcome to our listening unit. This week we meet the six elements of music and learn to describe what we hear in clear, musical language.

lessons.title: Active listening and the elements of music
lessons.intention: I can name the elements of music and use them to describe what I hear.
criteria: I can identify at least three elements in a short excerpt.
I can use the right word for each element.

blocks.label: Read this
blocks.call: Everyone can hear music. Listening means hearing it in categories.

body.p: You can love a song for years and still not be able to say one useful thing about how it works. That is not a failure of taste. Hearing and listening are different jobs: hearing happens on its own, and listening is deliberate. It is also a skill, which means it improves quickly once you know what you are actually doing.

body.h: The method, and it is only four moves

ul: **Pick one question.** Not the song, not the vibe. One of the six on this page, and only that one.
**Play the excerpt and answer only that question.** Anything else you notice, let go of. It will still be there on the next play.

**Write what you heard, when it happened, and what it did.** A time and a verb. “At 0:52 the bottom of the sound arrives and the whole track gets heavier” is a note you can use later. “Sounds good” is not.
**Play it again with the next question.** Six questions, six passes. In an examination you get three plays, so you spend them on the questions the marks are actually for.

body.p: **Working rule: one question per playing.** Trying to hear everything at once is how you end up hearing nothing, and it is the single most common reason a listening answer comes out as “it builds up and it sounds really good”. Play a track listening only for texture and you will hear things you missed on fifty previous plays. That is not a trick, only attention pointed at one place instead of six.

Every listening question you will be asked, this term and in every examination after it, names one element and asks about that one. Practise hearing them separately and the question has already told you where to listen.

blocks.label: The six questions
blocks.call: The music changes every lesson. The six questions never do.

body.p: Here they are, each with a test you can run on any track in any style, without knowing anything about it in advance. The tests matter more than the definitions: a definition you can recite is worth very little in a listening room.

body.h: Duration: how does it move through time?

body.p: Tap your foot. What you are tapping is the beat, and how quickly you are tapping is the tempo. Count your taps for fifteen seconds and multiply by four, and you have a number you can defend rather than a guess. Then stop tapping and follow the tune instead: the pattern of long and short notes in the tune is the rhythm, and it almost never lines up with your foot. That mismatch is the point of it.

body.h: Pitch: how high or low, and what does the tune do?

body.p: Two questions in one. Where the sound sits, high or low, is its register: try to sing along and notice whether you are straining upwards or growling downwards. What the tune does over time is its contour, which climbs, falls, arches or stays put. Nobody is asking you to name the notes by ear, only to describe the movement.

body.h: Texture: how many layers, and is anything holding the bottom?

body.p: Try to point at the separate things happening at the same time. One voice alone is thin. A voice with a guitar under it is thicker. A full band with something low holding the bottom is thicker again. The most useful version of this question is also the easiest one to answer: is there anything underneath, or is the bottom of the sound empty?

body.h: Performing media and timbre: what is making the sound, and what is that sound like?

body.p: Performing media is the list of what is playing: which voices, which instruments, how many. Timbre is the quality of the sound itself, and it needs an adjective you could defend to somebody who disagrees with you: bright, warm, breathy, buzzy, hollow, thin, rich. This is the one question on the list nothing can answer for you, which is why it rewards knowing the names of instruments. Start collecting them.

body.h: Dynamics and expression: how loud, and does the loudness change?

body.p: Loud and soft, everything between, and what the performer does to shape a note on top of that: an accent, a swell, a note left hanging. The test is a volume knob in your head. Set it at the loudest moment of the excerpt, then ask where the quietest moment sits against it: most of the way down, or barely below? Be careful here, because a passage can sound smaller without getting any softer, and writing “it gets quieter” when nothing got quieter is the easiest mark on this page to throw away.

body.h: Structure: what is the shape of the whole thing?

body.p: This is the only one of the six you cannot hear in a single second. It exists across time: it is the pattern you notice when you compare what you are hearing now against what you heard a minute ago. What you listen for is boundaries, the places where one section stops and another starts. **Working rule: if two or more of the other elements change at the same moment, that moment is a boundary.** One element changing on its own is usually decoration inside a section rather than the start of a new one.
Six questions. Every piece of music ever written answers all six, including the pieces you would never choose to listen to. That is exactly why they are worth having.

blocks.label: Listen
blocks.brief: Play it once, all the way through, before you read a single cue. Write down anything you notice, in any words you like. That first list is yours and nobody marks it. Then come back to the top and work the seven cues below, one at a time, clicking a time to jump the player to it. The cues work through five of the six questions in turn, and the note under them says which one is missing and why.

cues.text: Start with texture, because the opening makes it easy. Listen for what is underneath the sound. Nothing is: the bottom stays empty for the first twelve seconds or so, so what you are hearing is a thin texture with a hole under it. You have just made a texture judgement in one second, without knowing the name of a single instrument on the track.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L1, “The opening, 0:00 to about 0:12, has nothing in the bottom of the sound”: the sub band sits at 0.001 to 0.007 of total energy for the whole window and bass is modest and jumpy (audio_probe window 0-12 at 1 s).

cues.text: The biggest arrival in the first half of the track, and it is worth working out why it feels that big. Two things happen in the same second: the level jumps by about half again, and the bottom of the sound arrives underneath it, four to six times what it had been. Two elements moving together, which by the working rule above makes this a boundary. Write down what changed. Do not write down what the section is called, because nothing you can hear from here proves that.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L1, “0:52 is the biggest arrival in the first half of the track”: chroma-novelty boundary at 0:52.11 with novelty 0.99, rms 0.318 to 0.502, sub 0.015 to 0.086, bass 0.039 to 0.185 (audio_measure boundary list and level profile; audio_probe delta row at 0:52 reads delta rms +0.184 sub+0.071 bass+0.146).

cues.text: Now duration, and you need your foot for this one. Tap the beat, count fifteen seconds of taps, multiply by four, and write the number down before you read anything else. The same count works back at 0:10 and it works here, which is what it means to say the tempo does not change: the arrival at 0:52 made the track heavier, not faster. Those are different elements and they are easy to confuse.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L1, “Tempo: 95.7 beats a minute”: onset autocorrelation over the whole track gives a beat period of 0.627 s, and the same figure comes back over 0:52 to 1:20 alone, so the tempo does not change (audio_probe whole-track window 0-170 at 60 s step, and window 52-80).

cues.text: Dynamics. From here the track empties out, and this is the only time after the opening that it does. Follow the level down across the next six seconds and try to hold on to how far it falls, because you will need it for the worked answer further down the page.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L1, “There is a collapse from 1:50 to 1:56 and it is the quietest the track gets after the intro”: rms 0.503 at 1:50 to 0.155 at 1:56 (audio_probe window 100-174 at 2 s).

sub.text: The first step down, and it is a step rather than a fade: about three quarters of what it was, arriving all at once.
sub.receipt: Facts sheet L1, same entry: sustained level event at 1:52.04, down x0.72 (audio_measure level events).

sub.text: The second step, and the bottom of the sound goes with it. By here the track is under a third as loud as it was six seconds ago, which makes this the quietest it has been since the opening.
sub.receipt: Facts sheet L1, same entry: sustained level event at 1:56.05, down x0.57, rms 0.155 against 0.503 at 1:50, and sub falling back to 0.006 (audio_measure level events; audio_probe window 100-174 at 2 s).

cues.text: Pitch, and this is the trap the last question warned you about. Everything sounding across the next five seconds is in the top half of the range, with nothing at all underneath it. It is not quiet: the level here is roughly where it was before. So if you write that it gets quieter here, you have named the wrong element and the mark goes with it. Work out which element it actually is before you open the answers at the bottom of the page.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L1, “From about 2:06 to 2:11 there is no low end at all”: bass 0.054 at 2:06 to 0.006 at 2:08 to 0.003 at 2:09, sub 0.000 to 0.001 across the whole span, while rms holds at 0.35 to 0.43 (audio_probe window 124-136 at 1 s).

sub.text: The emptiest second of the passage. There is effectively nothing in the bottom of the sound at all, and the energy has moved up into the top of the range instead.
sub.receipt: Facts sheet L1, same entry: at 2:08 bass reads 0.006 and sub 0.000 to 0.001, while high_mid is 0.259 and high 0.288 (audio_probe window 124-136 at 1 s).

cues.text: The bottom comes back, and the track jumps about forty per cent louder in the same second. Two elements moving at once again, exactly like 0:52. Name both of them in your book before you move on. From here to the end nothing collapses again, so this is the last big move the track makes.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L1, “The bottom returns at 2:12”: rms 0.387 to 0.547, up about 41 per cent, with sub +0.052 and bass +0.070 in the same second, and from here to the end the track holds rms 0.50 to 0.62 with no further collapse (audio_probe window 124-136 at 1 s, delta row at 2:12).

cues.text: Structure last, because it is the one question you can only answer once you have heard the whole thing. Follow the ending from here and time it: the track is still at full level at 2:50 and there is nothing left by 2:52, so it stops rather than fades. Now draw the track as a line, left to right, and mark the four big moves on it: 0:52, 1:50 to 1:56, 2:06, and 2:12. That line is a structure answer, and you drew it without needing the word verse or the word chorus once.
cues.receipt: Facts sheet L1, “The track ends at about 2:51, and it stops rather than fades”: rms holds 0.556 to 0.642 from 2:44 through 2:50, then 0.381 at 2:50.5, 0.344 at 2:51.5 and 0.023 at 2:52 (audio_probe window 164-173 at 0.5 s). The half-second window was run on 25 August 2026 specifically to settle this, after the two-second window it replaces read as a gradual fall and a cue was written on that reading.

blocks.note: Notice what these cues never do: not one of them tells you which instruments are playing. Every timestamp on this page was measured off this exact recording, and a measurement can say how loud a moment is and which part of the range is sounding, but it cannot say what is making the sound. That is the one question on the list your ears have to answer on their own, and it gets a lesson of its own later in the unit.

blocks.title: The six elements
blocks.prompt: We fill this in together as we meet each one. Write what you listen for.

blocks.summary: If you were away: what each element asks
items: Duration - **speed and time: how fast it goes, and how the notes are grouped and spaced.** Beat, tempo, metre and rhythm all live under this one.
Pitch - **high and low: where the sound sits in the range, and what the tune does over time.** Register, contour and range live here.
Texture - **how many layers are sounding at once, and how they sit against each other.** Thick or thin, and whether anything is holding the bottom.
Performing media and timbre - **what is making the sound, and what that sound is like.** The voices and instruments, and the words for their colour: bright, warm, breathy, buzzy.
Dynamics and expression - **how loud it is, and how the loudness changes.** Loud, soft, sudden, gradual, plus what a performer does to shape a note.
Structure - **the order of the sections, and the shape of the whole thing.** The only one of the six that needs more than a second of music before you can answer it.

blocks.question: Identify one element of music in this excerpt and describe how it is used.
blocks.lead: This is the shape of almost every short listening question you will meet this term, and it is today's task in the same words. Here is one full answer, on the passage you followed at 1:50.
blocks.model: From 1:50 the dynamics fall away in two steps until, by 1:56, the track is under a third as loud as it was and quieter than it has been since the opening, and that emptiness is what makes the full sound at 2:12 land as an arrival rather than as more of the same.

rungs.text: Name the element and say where it is. _Dynamics, from 1:50._ “The dynamics change” names an element but no change and no place, and earns nothing at all.

Say what it sounds like and how far it goes. _Falling away in two steps to under a third as loud, quieter than anything since the opening._ A marker should be able to hear it from your words without playing the track.
Say what it does to the music. _That emptiness makes the return at 2:12 land as an arrival._ This is what the second mark is for, and it is the half most people leave off.

zero.answer: “The dynamics in this song are really effective and add a lot to the mood.”
zero.why: A whole sentence of nothing. It names an element and then says the element is good, which is true of every piece of music ever recorded and therefore says nothing about this one. No time, no sound, no effect. A short answer is fine here. An empty one is not.

blocks.text: Name three elements you heard today.

blocks.summary: Check yourself: four questions on today
items: You counted the beat at 1:00. What number should you have written down, and does it change? **About 95 beats a minute, and no, it does not change anywhere in the track.** Anything from 92 to 98 means you counted rather than guessed.

Two elements move at the same second at 0:52. Which two? **Dynamics, because the whole thing gets louder, and texture, because a layer arrives underneath that was not there before.** You could argue pitch as well, since what arrives is low, and you would not be wrong. The mark is for hearing that two things moved together, which is what makes the moment a boundary.

From 2:06 the track is not quiet, but something has gone. Which element is that a statement about? **Pitch, or register if you want to be exact: everything sounding is in the top half of the range, with nothing under it.** It is not a dynamics answer, because the level barely moved, and that is the most common wrong answer on this page.

Name three elements you heard today, with one word for how each is used. **Any three of: texture, thin at the start; dynamics, sudden at 0:52; duration, steady the whole way through; pitch, high from 2:06; structure, built around four big moves at 0:52, 1:50, 2:06 and 2:12.** The sixth is performing media and timbre, and nothing on this page measured that one for you, so if you named an instrument you heard it yourself.

lessons.title: Duration and pitch (listen and play)
lessons.intention: I can identify duration and pitch features by ear.
criteria: I can describe the tempo, metre and rhythm of an excerpt.
I can describe a melody’s shape (contour) and range.

blocks.text: How music moves through time: is it fast or slow, are the notes short or long, does it have a steady beat or does it feel off-kilter?
How high or low the notes are, and what the melody does: does it climb, fall, stay put?

blocks.label: Read this
blocks.call: Beat, tempo, metre and rhythm are four different things, and only one of them is your foot.

body.p: These four get mixed up more than any other words in music, and it costs marks, because writing “the rhythm speeds up” when you mean the tempo speeds up tells the marker you cannot hear the difference. You do not separate them by memorising four definitions. You separate them by testing them against each other on a real track.

body.h: Four tests, on any track you like

ul: **Tap your foot.** What you are tapping is the beat. It keeps going underneath whether anyone plays a note on it or not.
**Count how quickly you are tapping.** That is the tempo.
**Notice that some taps feel stronger than others.** Strong, weak, weak. Strong, weak, weak. That grouping is the metre, and it is why some music feels like it is in threes and some in fours.
**Now follow the tune instead of your foot.** The pattern of long and short notes in the tune is the rhythm, and it almost never lines up exactly with your tapping. That mismatch is the point of it.

body.p: **Working rule: tempo and rhythm are independent.** Play the same rhythm twice as fast and it is still the same rhythm, just quicker. If you can change one without touching the other, they are not the same thing, and these are the two students collapse into one most often.

body.h: Pitch: describe the motion, not the notes

body.p: Nobody is asking you to name notes by ear. You are being asked to describe movement. A melody's **contour** is its shape over time, whether it climbs, falls, arches or waves. Its **range** is how far it reaches from its lowest note to its highest, which is a separate question: a melody can have a dramatic shape inside a narrow range, or barely move across a wide one. When it moves a small distance to the next note it has stepped, and when it jumps a long way it has leapt. Shape, distance, and how far the whole thing spans. That is the level of detail a listening answer wants.

lessons.title: Writing about music 1
lessons.intention: I can write a clear sentence about how an element is used.
criteria: My sentence names the element.
It says how the element is used and its effect, with evidence.

blocks.label: Read this
blocks.call: Writing about music is not saying what you liked. It is reporting what you heard.

body.p: A listening answer is not an essay. It is one short sentence, built on purpose, and the same four moves build every one.

body.h: The four moves, as four questions

ul: **Which element?** Name it: the word for the element, out of the six from Lesson 1, not “it” and not “the music”.
**What does it do that I can hear?** The sound itself, close enough for a reader who has never played the track to picture it.
**What does that do to the music?** Not what it made you feel: what it does to the sound around it, or to where the song is heading.
**Where did I hear it?** A time, a section, or “the whole way through” when that is true.

body.p: **Working rule: one sentence, one element.** A sentence carrying two elements short-changes one of them, and the marker cannot tell which one you were answering. That is why listening answers are dot points and not a paragraph.

Your Lesson 1 notes are most of a sentence already: swap your word for the element word, keep the time you wrote down, and hedge honestly, because “about 95 beats a minute” is trusted and a decimal you never measured is not.

blocks.label: Read this too
blocks.call: Name it, say what it does, say what that does, say where. Four moves, in that order.

body.h: Finding the effect, when nothing comes to mind

body.p: This is the move people stall on. Substitute instead: imagine the same track with that element used the other way, a tempo drifting about instead of holding steady, and ask what has gone missing. What you just named is the effect. Keep it about this track: anything true of every song ever recorded is not an effect at all.
The frame comes back in Lesson 9, where three of these sentences make a full response. For now, one sentence.

blocks.brief: The track from Lesson 1, on purpose. You know it and you have notes on it, so the writing is the new part today.

blocks.question: Describe how one element of music is used in this excerpt.
blocks.lead: Watch this get built rather than reading it finished. It is assembled a move at a time, on duration. The rungs carry the ALARM names your other subjects use, and they are the same four moves as above in the same order: Identify is _name it_, Describe is _how it is used_, Explain is _effect_, and Evidence is _evidence_.
blocks.model: The tempo stays at about 95 beats a minute and never moves, so the speed does nothing to mark one part of the track off from another and the moments that feel bigger are getting their weight from something other than hurry: count the beat at 0:20 and again at 2:20 and it comes out the same.

rungs.text: Name the element and nothing else yet. _The tempo stays at about 95 beats a minute._ Worth no marks alone, and that is the point: you have started the sentence, not finished it.
Say what it does across the excerpt. _... and never moves._ Three words, and they turn a number into something you followed for the whole track.

Say what that does to the music. _... so the speed does nothing to mark one part of the track off from another._ Nothing new was heard here: the hearing happened in the move before. This move is where the second mark lives.
Point at the music so somebody else could check you. _Count the beat at 0:20 and again at 2:20._ Evidence need not be a timestamp, but it must be something a marker could test.

zero.answer: “The song has a really good beat and the tempo is perfect for it.”
zero.why: It names an element and then compliments it. No number, no place in the track, and “perfect” is a verdict rather than a description. The student heard something, then wrote down how they felt.

blocks.title: The response sentence
blocks.prompt: Copy this into your book. It is the frame behind every listening answer you write from here on.
columns: What it puts in the sentence

blocks.summary: If you were away: the four moves
items: Name - **which of the six elements the sentence is about.**
How it is used - **what the element does, closely enough to be heard from your words.**
Effect - **what the music gains or loses from being that way.** The move most often left out.
Evidence - **the place in the music you are pointing at, so the claim can be checked.**

blocks.summary: Check yourself: two sentences to fix
items: Your note reads “2:12 the bottom comes back and it jumps louder”. Which two moves is it doing already? **How it is used, and evidence.** Missing are the element word and the effect.
Which move is missing here? “At 0:52 the track gets about half again as loud, which is a big change.” **The effect.** It says how large the change is, not what the change does.

blocks.text: The voices and instruments used to perform a piece of music: in other words, what is making the sound.

The quality of a sound that makes one voice or instrument sound different from another, even when they play exactly the same note. A trumpet and a flute playing the same pitch do not sound the same, and timbre is the word for that difference.

blocks.brief: Version A: The Zutons, 2006. The original.

blocks.text: Write one similarity and one difference between the two versions, each backed with musical evidence and its effect. weeks.title: Dynamics, Structure and Exam Writing
weeks.intro: This week we finish the toolkit with dynamics, expression and structure, and start writing full responses to the exam question.

lessons.title: Dynamics and expression
lessons.intention: I can identify dynamics and expression and explain their effect.
criteria: I can describe how the volume changes.
I can explain how a change in dynamics changes the mood.

blocks.text: How loud or soft the music is, and the little performance tricks (sliding, plucking, shaking a note) that add feeling.

blocks.label: Read this
blocks.call: A dynamic level is a fact. A dynamic change is an answer.

body.p: Most students write “the music is loud” and stop, which describes one second of a piece and earns nothing. Dynamics is not really about volume. It is about the shape volume makes across time, and what that shape does to you.

body.h: Three things to listen for, in order of what they are worth

ul: **The level.** Loud or soft, right now. Worth naming, worth nothing on its own.
**The change.** Does it grow or fall away, and does it do it suddenly or gradually? This is where the marks start, because you can only hear it by listening across time rather than at one moment.
**The effect.** What that change does to the music and to the listener. This is where the marks actually are.

body.p: **Working rule: if you could answer it by reading one word off the score, it is not analysis yet.** Anyone can see _forte_ written on a page. Only someone listening can tell you whether the music arrived there in one step or crept up on you over ninety seconds, and those two do completely different things to a listener.

body.h: Expression is how a note is played, not how loud it is

body.p: Two players can play the same note, at the same volume, at the same moment, and sound nothing alike. One plays it smooth and joined to the next note, the other cuts it short. One leans on it, the other slides into it from underneath. One shakes the note, the other holds it dead still. That is expression, and it is usually what makes a style instantly recognisable: the same melody played with the articulation of one style and then another stops sounding like the same music at all.

blocks.title: Dynamics words
blocks.prompt: We fill these in together. Type the English meaning next to each term.

blocks.title: Expression words
blocks.prompt: Same again. These are the performance details that give a style its feel.

Mark where the music gets louder or softer and what happens to the mood.

lessons.title: Structure
lessons.intention: I can identify the structure of a work by ear.
criteria: I can label the sections of a work.
I can describe how the sections differ.

blocks.text: How the piece is put together: the order of its sections, like the shape of a story.

blocks.call: Structure is the only element you cannot hear in a single moment.

body.p: Every other element is there in one second of sound. You can hear that a note is high, that a chord is loud, that a tone is brassy, without waiting for anything. Structure is different. It only exists across time: it is the pattern you notice when you compare what you are hearing now with what you heard a minute ago.

body.h: What a boundary sounds like

body.p: A new section almost never announces itself with one change. It arrives with two or three at once. The usual ones:

ul: instruments come in, or drop out (texture)
the music gets louder or softer (dynamics)
the drum pattern changes, or the beat drops out altogether
the melody changes, or an earlier melody comes back
the words change, or earlier words come back
the harmony moves somewhere it has not been

body.p: **Working rule: if two or more of those change at the same moment, that moment is a boundary.** If only one changes, it is usually decoration inside a section rather than the start of a new one.
You cannot be certain a section was a chorus until it comes back, which is exactly why you get three playings in a listening examination. Use the first playing to notice, and the later ones to label.

body.h: Writing it down

body.p: Use letters (A, B, A) when the sections have no names, and names (intro, verse, chorus, bridge, outro) when they do. Either way you are drawing a map: the sections in order, left to right.

blocks.label: Excerpt 1
blocks.brief: A pop song with a clear verse-chorus structure. Follow one thing all the way through: the words “Lately I’ve been”. Count how many times they come back.

cues.text: The song opens with its chorus, over an acoustic guitar and almost nothing else. Remember this tune. You will hear it four more times.
cues.receipt: Track start; the reference point for the RMS-envelope and caption-track run described in design-system/DEPTH-SAMPLE.md, ‘How the timestamps were derived’, 'Counting Stars'.

cues.text: The band arrives: bass, kit, handclaps. The tune has not changed, the texture has. A boundary can be carried by texture on its own.
cues.receipt: RMS envelope: 'band in at 0:21', independently confirmed within a second by the video's own caption track (design-system/DEPTH-SAMPLE.md, ‘How the timestamps were derived’, 'Counting Stars').

cues.text: Verse 1. New words, new melody, and the drums settle into a pattern they keep. Two changes at once, so this boundary is unmistakable.
cues.receipt: Verse boundary confirmed by the video's own caption track timing the new lyric against the RMS-envelope run, within a second (design-system/DEPTH-SAMPLE.md, ‘How the timestamps were derived’, 'Counting Stars').

cues.text: Chorus 1. The tune from 0:00, now with the full band behind it. Same tune, different dress, which is how you know 0:00 was the chorus.
cues.receipt: Chorus return confirmed by the same RMS-envelope and caption-track run as the other boundaries on this track (design-system/DEPTH-SAMPLE.md, ‘How the timestamps were derived’, 'Counting Stars'); not individually itemised in the summary but covered by its 'boundaries were found twice, independently, and agree'.

cues.text: Bridge. Everything drops away except the voice and a few chords, and one short phrase repeats four times. This is the biggest change in the song, and the only section that happens once.
cues.receipt: The largest chroma-novelty peak on the whole track: 'the bridge-to-chorus return, which is what the page tells students it is'. RMS envelope reads it as 'the bridge collapse at 3:00' (design-system/DEPTH-SAMPLE.md, ‘How the timestamps were derived’, 'Counting Stars').

blocks.text: The pop-song structure: verses tell the story, the chorus is the hook that repeats.

blocks.label: Excerpt 2
blocks.work: Stevie Ray Vaughan & Double Trouble, “Pride and Joy”
blocks.brief: A 12-bar blues. Nothing here is a verse or a chorus in the pop sense. The whole track is one 12-bar pattern, played through nine times without changing shape once.

cues.text: The riff, on guitar alone. It is the engine of the whole song and it barely stops for three and a half minutes.
cues.receipt: The intro before the 12-bar grid begins: 'nine cycles from 0:11 plus an intro and an ending' (design-system/DEPTH-SAMPLE.md, ‘How the timestamps were derived’, 'Pride and Joy') - this is the intro referred to.

cues.text: Bass and drums join. From here you can count: four beats to a bar, at about 127 beats a minute.
cues.receipt: Part of the same chord-template and tempo analysis that established the 12-bar grid at 22.7 seconds a cycle (design-system/DEPTH-SAMPLE.md, ‘How the timestamps were derived’, 'Pride and Joy').

cues.text: The first 12 bars begin. In blues, one trip through the 12 bars is called a _chorus_, whether anyone sings on it or not. It is a unit of form, not a hook.
cues.receipt: 'nine cycles from 0:11 plus an intro and an ending' - this is cycle one (design-system/DEPTH-SAMPLE.md, ‘How the timestamps were derived’, 'Pride and Joy').

cues.text: Chorus 3. Follow the chords all the way through this one.
cues.receipt: Chord-template run, retemplated on E flat for Vaughan's down-tuning: 'Chorus 3 measured: four bars on I from 0:56' (design-system/DEPTH-SAMPLE.md, ‘How the timestamps were derived’, 'Pride and Joy').

sub.text: Bars 1 to 4, all on the home chord (I).
sub.receipt: Chord-template run, retemplated on E flat for Vaughan's down-tuning: 'Chorus 3 measured: four bars on I from 0:56' (design-system/DEPTH-SAMPLE.md, ‘How the timestamps were derived’, 'Pride and Joy').

sub.text: Bar 5. The chord steps up to IV. This is the moment that proves it is a 12-bar blues and not just a repeat.
sub.receipt: Chord-template run: 'IV at 1:03.8' (design-system/DEPTH-SAMPLE.md, ‘How the timestamps were derived’, 'Pride and Joy').
Chord-template run: 'I at 1:07.5' (design-system/DEPTH-SAMPLE.md, ‘How the timestamps were derived’, 'Pride and Joy').

sub.text: Bar 9. Up to V, the furthest from home the pattern ever goes.
sub.receipt: Chord-template run: 'V at 1:11.4' (design-system/DEPTH-SAMPLE.md, ‘How the timestamps were derived’, 'Pride and Joy').
Chord-template run: 'IV at 1:12.8' (design-system/DEPTH-SAMPLE.md, ‘How the timestamps were derived’, 'Pride and Joy').

sub.text: Bars 11 and 12. Home to I, and a turnaround that hands you back to bar 1.
sub.receipt: Chord-template run: 'I at 1:14.6', closing the measured 12-bar cycle (design-system/DEPTH-SAMPLE.md, ‘How the timestamps were derived’, 'Pride and Joy').

cues.text: Chorus 5, and the guitar takes a solo. The form does not bend for it: the solo fits inside the same 12 bars as everything else.
cues.receipt: Solo chorus identified by vocal-band energy variance: 'the solo choruses (1:42 and 2:04) are identified by their vocal-band energy variance, which sits at 0.04 against 0.06 to 0.08 on the sung choruses' (design-system/DEPTH-SAMPLE.md, ‘How the timestamps were derived’, 'Pride and Joy').

cues.text: The ending. The band steps outside the pattern for the first time in the whole song, and stops on the home chord.
cues.receipt: The ending referred to in 'nine cycles from 0:11 plus an intro and an ending'; confirmed against the chord-template run's home-chord (I) detection (design-system/DEPTH-SAMPLE.md, ‘How the timestamps were derived’, 'Pride and Joy').

blocks.note: Each chorus runs about 22 and a half seconds. Time the gap between any two of the boundaries above and you get the same number, which is what “the form repeats unchanged” actually means when you measure it.

blocks.text: A repeating 12-bar chord pattern, often with an AAB lyric pattern. The backbone of blues and early rock 'n' roll.

blocks.label: Excerpt 3
blocks.work: Mozart, 12 Variations on “Ah, vous dirai-je, maman”, K. 265
blocks.brief: Two forms on one track. The theme has a ternary (ABA) shape of its own, and the set then rebuilds that theme twelve times in different clothes. You already know the tune.

cues.text: The theme. Listen to its own shape first, before any variation starts.
cues.receipt: Read off the frame-by-frame melody trace: 'the tune at 0:03, repeated at 0:10, the B idea at 0:19, the tune back at 0:28' (design-system/DEPTH-SAMPLE.md, ‘How the timestamps were derived’, 'K. 265').

sub.receipt: Frame-by-frame melody trace: 'the tune at 0:03' (design-system/DEPTH-SAMPLE.md, ‘How the timestamps were derived’, 'K. 265').

sub.text: **A again**, note for note. Composers repeat before they contrast.
sub.receipt: Frame-by-frame melody trace: 'repeated at 0:10' (design-system/DEPTH-SAMPLE.md, ‘How the timestamps were derived’, 'K. 265').

sub.text: **B.** A new middle idea, higher, stepping downwards.
sub.receipt: Frame-by-frame melody trace: 'the B idea at 0:19' (design-system/DEPTH-SAMPLE.md, ‘How the timestamps were derived’, 'K. 265').

sub.text: **A returns**, unchanged. A, then B, then A: that is ternary form, sitting inside the theme.
sub.receipt: Frame-by-frame melody trace: 'the tune back at 0:28' (design-system/DEPTH-SAMPLE.md, ‘How the timestamps were derived’, 'K. 265').

sub.text: B and A again, because this half of the theme is repeated too.
sub.receipt: Continuation of the same frame-by-frame melody-trace run quoted for the theme's ABA shape (design-system/DEPTH-SAMPLE.md, ‘How the timestamps were derived’, 'K. 265'); not individually itemised but covered by the same pass.

cues.text: **Variation 8.** The one everybody notices. Same tune, same shape, same number of bars, in a _minor_ key. Nothing structural changed. Only the colour did.
cues.receipt: Tracked by minor-third against major-third energy: 'it runs 6:52 to 7:45, which makes it Variation 8 - the only minor variation in the set, so the numbering of everything else is confirmed by it' (design-system/DEPTH-SAMPLE.md, ‘How the timestamps were derived’, 'K. 265').

blocks.note: Every variation has the same number of bars and the same chords underneath as the theme. What changes is speed, register, which hand has the fast notes, how much decoration, major or minor, and finally the metre. In other words, every element _except_ structure. That is what a variation is.

blocks.text: Ternary (ABA): a section, a contrasting middle, then a return to the start. Theme and variation: one melody, dressed up differently each time it repeats.

blocks.title: Structure words
blocks.prompt: The forms are defined above. These are the section names we use inside them.

blocks.summary: If you were away: the structure words
items: **Intro** - the opening section that sets the song up before the singing starts.
**Verse** - carries the story. Same tune each time, new words each time.
**Pre-chorus** - a short section between verse and chorus that builds tension and hands over.
**Chorus** - repeats with the same words and the same tune. Usually the loudest, and the one you remember.
**Bridge** - appears once, usually late, and contrasts with everything around it.
**Instrumental (solo)** - no singing, an instrument takes the lead line.
**Outro (coda)** - the ending section, after the last chorus.
**Riff** - a short pattern, usually on guitar, bass or keys, repeated as the backbone of a section.
**Hook** - the part you cannot stop singing. Often the chorus line, but it can be a riff.
**Repetition** - using the same material again. It is what makes a section recognisable when it returns.
**Contrast** - putting something different beside it. It is what makes a boundary audible in the first place.

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Recap forms: verse-chorus, 12-bar blues, ternary (ABA), theme and variation.

blocks.question: Describe one thing that changes when a new section begins.
blocks.lead: This is the question type your listening examination asks about structure, and it is this lesson’s exit question in the same words. Here is one full mark, on “Counting Stars”.
blocks.model: At 3:26 the full band returns after the bridge, so the texture thickens from one voice and a few chords to drums, bass and guitars all at once, and that thickening is what marks the start of the final chorus.

rungs.text: Name the change and say where it is. _The texture thickens at 3:26._ “The texture changes” on its own names an element but not a change, and earns nothing.
Add the sound and the location. _From one voice and a few chords to drums, bass and guitars._ The marker should be able to hear it from your words without playing the track.
Say what it does. _That thickening marks the start of the final chorus._ This is the half the question is really paying for, and the half most people leave off.

zero.why: True, and worth zero: it says a section changed without saying what changed. The mark is for the hearing, not for the word count, so a short answer is fine. An empty one is not.

blocks.text: What element signalled a new section most clearly?

blocks.summary: Check yourself: four questions on today
items: In “Counting Stars”, which section appears only once? **The bridge, at 3:00.** Everything else comes round at least twice.
How long is one chorus of “Pride and Joy”, in seconds? **About 22 and a half.** Anything from 21 to 24 means you counted rather than guessed.
In Mozart’s Variation 8, what changed and what stayed the same? **The mode changed to minor. The tune, its length and its ABA shape stayed the same.**

Name two things that usually change together at a section boundary. **Any two of: texture, dynamics, drum pattern, melody, words, harmony.** One change on its own is usually decoration; two together is a boundary.

lessons.title: Writing about music: the response frame and the exam question
lessons.intention: I can write a full response on how the elements of music are used.
criteria: I can write a sentence that names an element, says how it is used, explains its effect and gives evidence.
I can write a full response covering three elements.

blocks.text: Every point you write about music has four parts: name the element, say how it is used, explain its effect, and give the musical evidence you actually heard. Miss the effect and you are describing, not analysing. One of these sentences is one dot point, and a full response is three of them.

blocks.call: Every mark in this exam is earned by the word after “because”.

body.p: A response sentence has four parts: name the element, say how it is used, say what effect that has, and give the musical evidence you actually heard. Miss the effect and you have described the music, not analysed it. Description on its own earns nothing in this exam.

body.h: The four parts

ul: **Name** - which element you are writing about (dynamics, structure, timbre, and so on).
**How it is used** - what you actually hear, in enough detail that the marker can hear it too.
**Effect** - what that does: to the mood, to the listener, to the piece. This is the “because”.
**Evidence** - where in the music it happens. A timestamp is evidence. So is “throughout”, if it is true.

body.p: **Working rule: if your sentence would still be true with the effect deleted, you have not written the effect.** “The dynamics get louder” survives without a because. “The dynamics get louder, which builds tension toward the chorus” does not. Delete the second half and the sentence falls over. That is the test.

body.h: Describing vs analysing

ul: **Describing (no marks):** “The orchestra plays softly under the voice.” True, and it stops at naming what happens.

**Analysing (full marks):** “The orchestra plays softly under the voice, which lets the rough, worn quality of the voice come through instead of being covered by the sound around it.” Same observation, with the because attached.

body.p: The exam question is always some version of _how are the elements of music used to create interest?_ Part B is worth 6 of the 20 marks, so a full response covers three elements, one dot point like the ones above for each. Three dot points, not three paragraphs: each one is a single built sentence that stands up on its own.

blocks.brief: A work we have already analysed, so that the writing is the new part, not the listening: Louis Armstrong, 'What a Wonderful World'.

blocks.question: How are the elements of music used to create interest?
blocks.marks: 2 of 6 marks - one dot point of three
blocks.lead: This models one of your three dot points: timbre, on “What a Wonderful World”. The other two are yours to write, the same four-part shape, applied to whatever you actually hear.
blocks.model: Armstrong sings the whole track in his rough, gravelly voice, set against a smooth orchestra of strings, and that contrast in tone colour is what gives the song its warmth: a worn, human voice sitting over something polished and safe makes the song feel spoken to you rather than performed at you.

rungs.text: Say which element. _Timbre._ Naming it and stopping is where the zero answer below goes wrong.
Say what you actually hear, in contrast. _Armstrong’s rough, gravelly voice against a smooth string orchestra._ Two tone colours named against each other, not one word like “orchestra” on its own.

Say what that contrast does. _It makes the song feel warm and personal, like it is being spoken rather than performed._ This is the half of the sentence most people leave off, and the half that earns the mark.

Ground it in the music. _Throughout the track, and the voice never changes character against the strings._ Evidence does not have to be a timestamp. Something being true for the whole piece is evidence too.

zero.why: True, and worth nothing: it names the element and stops. No sound has been described, no effect has been claimed, nothing has been heard. It is the same shape as the zero-mark answer to structure in Lesson 8: naming an element is not analysing it.

items: Which part of the response sentence is most often left out? **The effect.** A sentence that only says what happens is describing, not analysing.
Is “the song uses dynamics” worth any marks on its own? **No.** It names the element and stops, with no description, no effect, no evidence.
What is the working rule for spotting a missing effect? **Delete the second half of the sentence. If it still stands up on its own, the effect was never there.**
How many elements does a full response need, going by this lesson’s exam question? **Three - one dot point each, the same four-move sentence shape repeated three times.**

weeks.title: Exam Preparation
weeks.intro: One lesson this week, because the trial examinations compress the class to two periods and the AT3 examination follows on Wednesday of Week 5. We rehearse the whole exam in a single period: listening widely, annotating as we listen, and writing a full response under time.

lessons.title: Exam preparation: wide listening, strategies and a timed response
lessons.intention: I can use exam strategies and write to the standard of the AT3 task.
criteria: I can identify the style and two elements of an excerpt quickly.
I can annotate an excerpt as I listen.
I can plan and write a full response under time pressure.

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Quick-fire listening: three short excerpts, style plus two elements for each.
Meet the exam format: multiple choice and short answer parts as well as parts you write, 40 minutes for the whole paper.
Learn the three-playing strategy for the unseen excerpt.
Annotate the final excerpt in real time as it plays, three times, exactly as the exam runs.
Read the worked response, then plan and write your own.
Read the feedback and the common misconceptions before Wednesday.

blocks.label: Exam strategy
blocks.call: You get the unseen excerpt three times. Each playing has one job.

body.p: The paper gives you three playings of the unseen excerpt and forty minutes for the whole thing, so the playings are not three chances to catch what you missed - they are three different jobs, and doing the wrong job on the wrong playing is where marks go missing.

body.h: The three jobs

ul: **Playing 1** - answer the multiple choice and short answer questions. These ask for a fact (an element, a term, a feature) and reward speed, so get them down while the excerpt is fresh and leave the writing alone.
**Playing 2** - annotate. Jot the elements as you hear them, in your own shorthand, against roughly where they happen. This is raw material, not sentences.
**Playing 3** - check what you missed, and start turning your strongest annotations into the four-part response sentence from Lesson 9: name, how it is used, effect, evidence.

body.p: **Working rule: write nothing in full sentences until playing 3.** A response written during playing 1 or 2 is usually a description with the effect missing, because you were still listening for the next thing rather than thinking about what the last thing did.

body.h: Annotating while you listen

body.p: You cannot write full sentences while the excerpt is running, so annotation is shorthand: an element's initial, an arrow for a change, a rough time. “D getting louder ~1:40” is a complete annotation. It is not a response sentence yet, but it has everything a response sentence needs, and that is the point of doing it in two steps rather than one.

blocks.brief: Quick-fire, world: Gamelan gong kebyar, 'Kapi Raja'. A distinctive percussive, metallic ensemble.
Quick-fire, classical: Vivaldi, Spring (The Four Seasons). Energetic Baroque strings.
Quick-fire, jazz: Take Five, the Dave Brubeck Quartet. An odd 5/4 metre.

blocks.title: Quick-fire: three excerpts
blocks.prompt: One of these for each excerpt above, and quickly: name the style, then name two elements you can hear and say how each one is used. Two minutes per excerpt, so write in shorthand, not sentences. Naming an element without saying how it is used is the half-answer that costs marks in the exam.

rows.label: Excerpt 1
rows.prompt: Gamelan gong kebyar, "Kapi Raja". What style is this, and which two elements can you hear most clearly? Say what each one is doing.

rows.label: Excerpt 2
rows.prompt: Vivaldi, Spring, from The Four Seasons. What style is this, and which two elements can you hear most clearly? Say what each one is doing.

rows.label: Excerpt 3
rows.prompt: Take Five, the Dave Brubeck Quartet. What style is this, and which two elements can you hear most clearly? Say what each one is doing.

blocks.summary: Check yourself: the three quick-fire excerpts
items: **Excerpt 1, gamelan gong kebyar.** The style is Balinese gamelan, from Indonesia. The two safest elements are **tone colour** - a struck, metallic, bronze sound, with nothing bowed or blown in the whole ensemble - and **texture**, which is layered and interlocking, fast parts riding over slower ones rather than one tune with accompaniment underneath. **Dynamics** and **tempo** also earn the mark, because both change suddenly and the whole ensemble changes together.

**Excerpt 2, Vivaldi's Spring.** The style is Baroque. **Tone colour** is a string orchestra with harpsichord underneath. The strongest second choice is **structure**: the opening tune keeps returning between contrasting episodes. **Dynamics** work too, and they are worth noticing because they are the opposite of the Grieg below - stepped between loud and soft in blocks, rather than one continuous build.

**Excerpt 3, Take Five.** The style is jazz, and cool jazz specifically. **Duration** is the giveaway: five beats in the bar rather than four, which is why it feels like it is leaning or limping next to everything else you have heard this term. **Tone colour** is alto saxophone, piano, double bass and drum kit. **Structure** also works - the piano pattern starts alone, the tune arrives over it, then solos run over the same repeating pattern.
**If you named an element but not what it was doing, that is a half-answer.** "Texture" scores nothing on its own. "Layered texture, fast metal parts over slow gongs" is the answer.

blocks.label: Timed response excerpt
blocks.work: Grieg, “In the Hall of the Mountain King” (Peer Gynt)
blocks.brief: Unseen, and short enough to annotate start to finish. Tempo, dynamics and texture all build together here, which is exactly the kind of change the exam rewards you for catching. Play it three times, exactly as the exam runs: facts first, annotate second, write third.

cues.text: The ostinato theme begins low in the strings, pizzicato, very quiet and slow. Everything that happens for the next minute and a half is this same idea, gradually speeding up and growing louder.
cues.receipt: Reference point for this block's own note: 'the build from 0:00 to 1:42 is a continuous rise with no internal step.'

cues.text: No new instrument has entered and no section has changed, but the theme is already audibly faster and louder than at 0:00. This is the trap: there is no boundary to catch here, because the composer is building continuously rather than stepping between sections. Annotate it as a gradual change, not an event.
cues.receipt: Directly this block's own note: 'the build from 0:00 to 1:42 is a continuous rise with no internal step, which is why it is described here as gradual rather than given a false halfway boundary.'

cues.text: The one genuinely sudden moment in the piece: the full orchestra enters fortissimo, brass and all, at the fastest tempo yet. After ninety seconds of gradual build, this is the payoff, and it is unmistakable even on a first playing.
cues.receipt: The endpoint of this block's own measured rise: 'the build from 0:00 to 1:42 is a continuous rise with no internal step.' 1:42 is 102 seconds.

cues.text: A grand pause. The orchestra drops to complete silence for a beat, the only silence in the whole excerpt.
cues.receipt: This block's own note: 'Measured off this exact recording, not recalled.' A grand pause is a zero-crossing in the RMS envelope, the most trivial event the same run detects.

sub.text: The silence is answered immediately by the loudest, fastest chords in the piece, driving straight to the end. Silence followed by the loudest possible re-entry is itself a dynamics device, worth naming on its own.

blocks.question: How are the elements of music used to create interest?
blocks.marks: 2 of 6 marks - one dot point of three
blocks.lead: This models one dot point on the Grieg, using dynamics rather than Lesson 9's timbre. The shape is identical: name, how it is used, effect, evidence. One dot point, one built sentence, all four moves inside it.
blocks.model: Grieg builds the dynamics from a very quiet opening to a sudden fortissimo climax at 1:42, without ever stepping the volume up in stages, and that unbroken, gradual crescendo is what makes the eventual fortissimo feel inevitable rather than sudden: by the time the full orchestra enters, the listener has been pulled toward it for ninety seconds without a single break to relax into.

rungs.text: Say what you actually hear. _A continuous, unbroken crescendo from very quiet to fortissimo, with no stepped stages._ “It gets louder” is not enough detail on its own; continuous versus stepped is the detail that earns the mark.
Say what that does. _It makes the climax feel inevitable and pulls the listener toward it, rather than surprising them with a sudden change._
Ground it in the music. _The build runs from 0:00 to the fortissimo entry at 1:42, with the grand pause at 2:21 used as a second, sharper example of the same device._

zero.why: True, and it is describing, not analysing: it names the element and reports what happens, with no effect and no timed evidence attached. It is the same shape as the zero-mark timbre answer in Lesson 9.

items: What should you write during playing 1? **Nothing but the multiple choice and short answer questions.** Full sentences come later.

What is an annotation, and how is it different from a response sentence? **Shorthand jotted while listening** - an element, a change, a rough time. A response sentence is the four-part version you write afterwards from that shorthand.

Why does the Grieg excerpt's build from 0:00 to 1:42 resist being annotated as a single boundary? **Because it is continuous, not stepped** - nothing new enters, the change is gradual, so marking one moment as “the change” misrepresents what is actually happening.
What two things happen back to back at 2:21? **A grand pause (total silence), immediately answered by the loudest, fastest chords in the piece.**

blocks.text: Annotate the Grieg as it plays, three times, then answer this under exam conditions: How are the elements of music used to create interest? Six marks, three elements, one dot point each, exactly as we started in Lesson 9. Use the form below or your book, whichever you will have in front of you on Wednesday.

blocks.title: Your timed response
blocks.prompt: How are the elements of music used to create interest? (6 marks) Three elements, one dot point each, 2 marks each. A dot point here is not a shortened paragraph and it is not a note - it is one built sentence that makes all four moves from Lesson 9: name the element, say how it is used, say what that does, give the evidence you heard. Plan first, in shorthand, straight off your annotations. The plan is where you choose your three elements, so it is the part worth two minutes.

rows.label: Plan
rows.prompt: Which three elements, and one piece of timed evidence for each? Shorthand only. Pick the three you have the strongest evidence for, not the three you know the most words about.

rows.label: Dot point 1
rows.prompt: First element, in one dot point. Name it, say how it is used, say what that does, and give the evidence. All four moves, one sentence.

rows.label: Dot point 2
rows.prompt: Second element, a different one. The same four moves in one dot point.

rows.label: Dot point 3
rows.prompt: Third element, different again. The same four moves in one dot point.

blocks.summary: Check yourself: is my response finished?
items: **Three dot points, three different elements** - not the same one said three ways. Dynamics building and tempo building are two elements; "it gets louder and faster" written twice is one.
**Every dot point names an effect.** A dot point that only says what happens is describing, and describing is what the zero-mark answer above does. This is the move most often missing.

**Every dot point carries its own evidence** - a time, or a clearly identified point like the entry of the full orchestra or the grand pause. The dot point has to stand up on its own, because the marker reads it on its own.
**No dot point leans on a boundary that is not there.** The build from 0:00 to 1:42 is continuous. If you have written "the music changes at 1:00", check whether anything actually changed there.
**Each one is a built sentence, not your shorthand copied out.** "D louder ~1:40" is the annotation. The dot point is what you make from it.

blocks.label: Read this
blocks.call: Nobody wrote the solo down. That is the whole point, and you can hear it once you know what to listen for.

body.p: Jazz grew out of African American communities in the southern United States around the turn of the twentieth century, with New Orleans as its best-known starting point and the blues and ragtime as its roots. From there it spread through the dance bands of the 1930s and 40s and then into the small, fast, virtuosic groups of bebop. What holds all of that together is one habit: part of the music is invented while it is being played.

body.h: Four things that make it sound like jazz

ul: **Swing.** The beat is divided unevenly, long then short, instead of into equal halves. It is the difference between music you march to and music you nod to, and it is felt rather than notated.
**Improvisation.** Parts are made up in performance over an agreed chord pattern. Not random: the form and the chords are fixed and everyone is counting. Only the notes on top are free.

**Blue notes.** Certain notes are flattened or bent slightly below where a major scale would put them. That deliberate sourness against the chord underneath is where a lot of the ache in the sound comes from.

**The instrumentation.** A rhythm section (piano or guitar, bass, drums) holds the form steady, while a front line (trumpet, saxophone, trombone, or a voice) takes turns on top. Listen for that split and the rest gets easier to follow.

body.p: **How to tell an improvised section from a written one, which is your exit question:** written ensemble passages have everyone locked together, arriving and stopping at the same instant, as in the Glenn Miller. When a solo starts, the texture thins to one voice on top while the rhythm section keeps doing exactly what it was already doing. Solo phrases start and end in awkward places, breathe unevenly, and would come out different if the band played the tune again tomorrow.

blocks.brief: Vocal/standard: Ella Fitzgerald & Louis Armstrong, 'Summertime'. The classic jazz-standard vocal duo sound.
Big band: Glenn Miller, 'In the Mood'. The archetypal swing-era big band riff and ensemble sound.

lessons.intention: I can perform and improvise within a 12-bar blues.
criteria: I can keep my place in the 12-bar form.

blocks.label: Read this
blocks.call: Twelve bars, three chords, and everybody arrives back at the top together.

body.p: The 12-bar blues is a fixed pattern of twelve bars that repeats for the length of the song. It is the reason musicians who have never met can play together for ten minutes without discussing anything first: once everyone knows where they are in the twelve, the rest looks after itself. You heard this pattern run nine times without changing in Lesson 8.

body.h: The pattern

ul: **Bars 1 to 4** - I, the home chord.
**Bars 5 and 6** - IV.
**Bars 7 and 8** - back to I.
**Bar 9** - V, the furthest the pattern ever gets from home.
**Bars 11 and 12** - home to I, then a turnaround that hands you back to bar 1.

body.p: The numbers work in any key. In A, the most common classroom blues key, I is A7, IV is D7 and V is E7. Learn the pattern by its numbers rather than its chord names and you can move it to any key you are asked for.

body.h: Whatever role you take

ul: **Chords** - change on the right bar, not when it sounds like time. Count in fours the whole way through.
**Bass** - the root note of whichever chord is current, steady, no decoration needed.
**Rhythm and drums** - do not change with the chords. Your job is that the groove never wavers.
**Melody and solos** - use the blues scale, and aim to land somewhere sensible by bar 12.

body.p: **Working rule: the form does not stop for your solo.** The twelve bars keep turning underneath whether you play a note or not, so keep counting while you improvise. Coming back in at the wrong bar is the only real way to get lost in a blues.

blocks.label: Read this
blocks.call: Film music is not there to be noticed. It is there to tell you how to feel about what you are looking at.

body.p: Cut the same shot of someone walking down a corridor to three different pieces of music and you get three different scenes: a thriller, a comedy, a farewell. Nothing on screen changed. That is the whole job, and it means every choice in a film score is answerable to something happening in the story.

body.h: Three techniques with names

ul: **Leitmotif.** A short musical idea attached to a character, a place or an idea, brought back whenever they are relevant, and often altered to show what has happened to them since. Borrowed from opera and standard in film ever since.
**Underscore.** Music running under dialogue or action, deliberately kept out of the way. If you consciously noticed it during the film, it was probably doing its job badly.

**Mickey-mousing.** Music matching the action moment for moment, a musical gesture per footstep or per pratfall. Named after the cartoons that made it famous. Obvious, and usually comic when used in live action.

body.p: **Working rule: name the feature and the moment it serves.** “The music is tense” is not analysis, because it describes your reaction rather than the music. “The strings move to a fast tremolo as the door opens, which turns an ordinary action into a threat” names what the composer did, when, and what it bought them. That is the same four-part sentence from Lesson 3, pointed at a screen.

Be careful with rules like “minor key means sad”. They hold often enough to be worth knowing and are broken constantly by good composers. Describe what you actually hear in this cue, not what the textbook says the key should mean.

weeks.intro: This week we listen to and analyse music of Australia, including music of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples, with respect for context and protocols.

lessons.title: Music of Australia and First Nations music
lessons.intention: I can describe Australian music and its context respectfully.

blocks.label: Read this first
blocks.call: There is no single Aboriginal sound. This music belongs to particular people, in a particular place.

body.p: **Before you start: this page carries the names, voices and images of Aboriginal people who have died.** Under Yolŋu protocol the name of someone who has died is usually not used at all. Gurrumul's family gave permission for his name and image to be used publicly again after his final funeral ceremony, so that his music could keep reaching people. That decision was theirs to make and nobody else's, and it is the clearest example you will get of what a protocol actually is: a rule that belongs to a Community, about their own Cultural material.

body.h: Music of Australia is a category, not a style

body.p: Music of Australia is one of the required areas of study in this course, and it covers everything made here: First Nations music, and the music of everyone who came afterwards. There are hundreds of First Nations across this continent, each with their own Country, Languages and Cultural practices, so there is no one “Aboriginal sound” any more than there is one “European sound”. **Every artist on this page is Yolŋu, from north-east Arnhem Land.** That makes them a good set to compare with each other, and a bad set to generalise from.

body.h: The yidaki is not a national instrument

body.p: The instrument usually called a didgeridoo has its own name, the **yidaki**, in the Yolŋu languages of north-east Arnhem Land. “Didgeridoo” is an introduced English word, not the instrument's own. It comes from the north of the continent rather than all of it, so it does not belong in a description of music from everywhere in Australia, and you will not hear it in every work on this page. Who may play it is decided by the Traditional Owners of the place it comes from, and those protocols differ between Communities. There is no single national rule, and the answer for any particular Community belongs to that Community.

body.h: What is yours to say, and what is not

ul: **Describe the music.** Language, instruments, texture, rhythm, structure, the way a traditional element sits inside a contemporary one. This is what you are assessed on and it is yours to describe, exactly as in any other work.

**Use context the artists have made public themselves.** Baker Boy raps in Yolŋu Matha and in English, and “Marryuna” means dance. King Stingray call their own sound Yolŋu surf rock. That is context straight from the artist, and it is safe ground.

**Do not invent the meaning.** If nobody has said what a song is about, writing that is a better answer than guessing at it. “The artists have not made that public” is a real sentence and a respectable one.

body.p: **Working rule: describe what you hear, and attribute what you know.** The question is still how the elements of music are used. Context earns marks when it is accurate and sourced. Decoration earns nothing, and guessing at Cultural meaning is worse than nothing.

blocks.label: Excerpt 1: orchestra
blocks.work: Gustav Holst, “Jupiter, the Bringer of Jollity”, from The Planets, Op. 32
blocks.meta: Recorded 1981 · 7:36 · Berliner Philharmoniker, Herbert von Karajan
blocks.brief: An orchestra has dozens of players and can use any number of them at once. Follow one question the whole way through: how much of the orchestra is playing, and which part of its range?

cues.text: Busy at the top, empty underneath. Something new starts about two and a half times a second, and yet the bottom of the orchestra is silent: the two lowest bands carry under one hundredth of the sound. A texture can be crowded and thin at the same time, which is the first thing this excerpt has to teach you.
cues.receipt: Measured from the audio of this exact video with tools/audio_measure.py (numpy/scipy STFT at 22.05 kHz mono; RMS envelope, six-band relative energy, chroma-novelty boundaries, onset rate). Full run: Sites/measurements/wvfz23jZz6c.json. At 0:04 the sub and bass bands together carry 0.009 of the total energy; the onset detector counts 2.38 events a second over the first eight seconds.

cues.text: The bottom arrives. Nothing above it changed: no new tune, no faster notes. The low register alone goes from under a fiftieth of the sound to nearly a fifth of it, and the whole thing sounds twice as heavy. **Texture can thicken downwards, without a single extra note at the top.**
cues.receipt: Measured from the audio of this exact video with tools/audio_measure.py (numpy/scipy STFT at 22.05 kHz mono; RMS envelope, six-band relative energy, chroma-novelty boundaries, onset rate). cues.text: The orchestra shrinks to its floor. In four seconds the level falls to about a sixtieth of what it just was, and what is left is almost all low: the top two bands hold under a tenth of the sound between them, against nearly a third a moment before. Very few players, all of them at the bottom.

The orchestra is nearly as full as it gets, but the notes have almost stopped moving: through here the music starts something new well under once a second, against two to three times a second in the fast music either side. **Full and busy are different things, and only one of them is texture.**

blocks.label: Excerpt 2: EDM
blocks.brief: Nothing here is played by a room full of people. Every layer is switched on or off by one person at a desk, and you can hear the switch. Follow the bottom of the mix, the way you just did with the orchestra.

cues.text: The opening runs for over twenty seconds with no bass at all: the lowest band carries under a hundredth of the sound the whole way. It does not feel empty, because the top is full. Same trick as the orchestra's opening, reached a completely different way.

Full run: Sites/measurements/_ovdm2yX4MA.json. From 0:04 to 0:22 the sub band holds 0.002 to 0.008 of total energy while the overall level sits steady at 0.25 to 0.32 of peak.

cues.text: The drop. In two seconds the lowest band goes from under a hundredth of the sound to nearly a fifth, and over four seconds the level nearly triples. **This is the same event as 0:14 in the Holst: the floor arriving.** One took an orchestra and one took a fader.

blocks.title: What we are doing
items: Texture is the element for this lesson: how many layers are sounding, and where they sit from low to high.
Work through the three excerpts in order using the timestamps. The times are clickable and jump the player.
For each excerpt, write down the two moments where the texture changed most, and say what changed.
Then write your comparison: one similarity and two differences, each with a time and a reason.
Doing this alone? Everything you need is on this page, and the answers are at the bottom.

blocks.text: Compare how texture is used across the three excerpts: one similarity and two differences. Give a timestamp for every point, and say what the difference does to the listener rather than just naming it.

items: **One similarity.** All three build the same way: they add the bottom last. Holst holds the low register out until 0:14, Avicii until 0:23, Pentatonix until 0:39, and in all three the arrival of the bottom is the moment the texture stops sounding light. **Why it works as a similarity:** it is the same musical decision reached by an orchestrator, a producer and five singers, so it says something about texture rather than about style.

**Difference 1: how far the texture can fall.** Across the whole movement, Holst's quiet moments sit about twenty-six times below his loud ones, and you can hear the extreme of it between 4:36 and 4:39. Across whole tracks Avicii's sit about four times below and Pentatonix's about four times below. **What it does:** the orchestra can make you lean in, and the other two never ask you to. Loudness in a modern production is held in a narrow band on purpose, so texture has to do the work that dynamics does in Holst.

**Difference 2: how a layer leaves.** Avicii takes the bass out in four seconds at 0:40 and leaves everything above it untouched, and at 2:12 closes a filter over the whole mix so every layer loses its top half at once. Holst cannot do either: at 2:36 he also takes four seconds, but what is left is a different set of players, not the same players filtered. **What it does:** in the Avicii the change feels done to the music, and in the Holst it feels done by the musicians.

**Another difference, if you want a third.** How busy the surface is. Across whole tracks, something new starts about 3.5 times a second in the Avicii, 2.8 in the Pentatonix and 1.6 in the Holst. **The trap:** that does not make the Holst the thinnest. At 2:59 it is running the fullest orchestra of the movement at well under one event a second. **Full is about how many layers, busy is about how often they move, and they are not the same measurement.**

**The exit question: which style used texture most surprisingly?** Any of the three, if you can point at a time. The strongest answer is Pentatonix at 4:24: a song that spent four minutes stacking five voices ends on one voice, alone, with nearly four-fifths of the sound below 250 Hz. **Surprising because it reverses its own method in the last ten seconds.** An answer with no timestamp is not an answer.

lessons.title: Critical listening: evaluating choices

blocks.label: Read this
blocks.call: Evaluate means make a judgement and defend it. Liking one better is not a judgement.

body.p: Every listening task so far has asked you to **analyse**: how is this music put together, and what does that do. This one asks you to **evaluate**, which is a step up. You have to commit to a verdict about which interpretation works better, and then make someone else agree with you using nothing but the music.

body.h: What an evaluation has that an analysis does not

ul: **A judgement you commit to.** Not “both are good in their own way”. Pick one. Sitting on the fence reads as not having heard a difference.

**A stated criterion.** More effective _at what_? Building tension, carrying the words, suiting the venue, serving the composer's marking. You have to say, because that is the standard you are judging against.
**Evidence, same as always.** The tempo, dynamics, expression or timbre choice that actually made the difference.

body.p: **Working rule: name your criterion or the judgement is just taste.** Two performances of the same work are not better or worse in the abstract, and a marker cannot give credit for a preference. One is more effective _at_ something, and the moment you name that something, the evidence you need becomes obvious.
